analysis.one_liner: Lets states cap how long freight trains can block road crossings.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: referred in August 2024, sent to the railroads subcommittee the next day, and given no hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: When a freight train sits parked across a road crossing, drivers, delivery trucks, school buses, and emergency vehicles can be stuck for long stretches, and state laws that try to limit how long a railroad may block a crossing have been struck down as overridden by federal law. This bill would change federal law so states could set and enforce their own limits on blocked crossings. It was introduced by one Ohio Republican, got no cosponsors, was never taken up by the committee it was sent to, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, commuters, truckers, and emergency responders who are currently stuck at road crossings when freight trains park on them. Communities near busy rail lines would gain the power to set waiting limits and enforce them, instead of seeing state laws struck down in court as preempted by federal law [S2, S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and communities at rail crossings

how_it_helps.text: It would let states adopt or enforce laws limiting the duration that a railroad may block a highway-rail grade crossing, a power federal law has largely taken away.
Federal courts have generally found state anti-blocking laws preempted, rendering them unenforceable; the bill removes that preemption so communities can actually enforce waiting limits.

analysis.who_pays: Freight railroads, which would face state-by-state limits on how long trains can block a crossing, limiting their flexibility to hold cars in place while switching or waiting [S2, S3].

drawbacks.text: A national freight network would operate under a patchwork of 50 different state rules on how long a train may block a crossing, which railroads argue complicates operations across state lines.

The bill addresses only one rail problem — blocked crossings — and does nothing about other rail safety and service issues, such as train length or blocking of pedestrian crossings, leaving the underlying service complaints in place.

With no cosponsors and no committee action, the bill did not build any record of debate, so there is no evidence that a workable compromise between state authority and uniform national rail operations was ever explored.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and falls on people with no power in the deal: drivers whose time is taken, and communities whose emergency vehicles can be trapped by parked trains. The cost is that railroads would face many different state rules instead of one national standard, and this bill offers no national framework of its own — it simply opens the door to state laws. That is a modest, honest trade, but the bill was written narrowly (it touches only crossing blockage) and drew no cosponsors, which limited its political lift.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its railroads subcommittee and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 2, 2024 and referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day.
On August 3, 2024 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials, and no further action was recorded.
The 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025 with the bill still sitting in committee, so it is dead.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Freight railroads, which keep the freedom to leave trains blocking road crossings that this bill would have curtailed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Freight railroads, which keep blocking-crossing freedom

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — after it was referred on August 2, 2024.

against.name: Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on August 3, 2024 and never scheduled it for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a single Republican with no cosponsors from either party, and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would let states cap how long freight trains may block highway crossings, ending the operational freedom railroads have had to leave cars parked on crossings while switching or waiting. Drivers, commuters, and emergency responders are the people currently absorbing that cost.
Less time stuck at blocked crossings means faster freight deliveries and lower costs when trucks sit waiting at rail crossings.
